findings.title: Clinical state machine is entity-agnostic by construction
findings.description: transition(current, target, entity=...) uses 'entity' only for the error message; one flat dict governs blood units, orders, samples, crossmatches, transfusions and reactions. Any state name shared by two entity types collides.
findings.root_cause: No per-entity keying in the state machine design.
findings.evidence: Measured, not argued. Four state values are shared by more than one entity enum: 'completed' (DonationStatus, TransfusionStatus), 'in_progress' (DonationStatus, TransfusionStatus), 'expired' (ComponentStatus, DonorStatus), 'discarded' (ComponentStatus, DonationStatus). Three of the four are keys in the shared table, so one entity's rules silently govern another's — a donation in progress is validated against transfusion rules. Twenty-eight table keys are not any enum value at all: 'issued_order', 'received_sample', 'testing_crossmatch', 'ordered_transfusion' and others are synthetic names invented to dodge collisions, which is the workaround made visible. NR-004 and NR-020 are both instances of this. BATCH-2.5 measured the full registry: 39 table keys, 43 distinct vocabulary, 5 lifecycle enums, 4 colliding states (3 of them live keys), 28 synthetic keys, 18 enum values with no key at all, and — the sharpest number — exactly 2 distinct entity values are ever passed at a call site ('blood_unit', 'transfusion'), so the rows keyed for orders, samples, crossmatches and reactions govern nothing today and would govern the wrong thing once wired up. Four synthetic keys (issued_order, received_sample, testing_crossmatch, ordered_transfusion) are explicit <state>_<entity> compounds — (entity, state) keying already implemented by hand inside the string. BATCH-2.6 CORRECTION: the claim that 'a donation in progress is validated against transfusion rules' is wrong. Only two entity values are ever passed to transition(): blood_unit (11 call sites) and transfusion (2). crossmatch, donation and donor are never validated by the state machine at all, so no cross-entity mis-validation happens today. NR-007 is a latent trap that fires when a new entity is wired up — the mechanism of NR-004 and NR-020 — not an active defect. ATTRIBUTION: for each of the four colliding states exactly one claimant reaches the machine, so the live row provably belongs to it — completed and in_progress to transfusion, expired and discarded to blood_unit. No migration is required: no colliding value is a server_default on a Blood Bank table.
findings.clinical_impact: A future duplicate state name silently widens or blocks a clinical transition, as already happened once.
findings.security_impact: None directly.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Invalid transitions may be permitted across entity types.
findings.operational_impact: Fixes require union semantics that over-permit (current residual risk).
findings.recommended_fix: Key transitions by (entity, state) and fail closed on an unknown entity. The keying is mechanical; attributing the 28 synthetic keys and the 4 colliding states to entities is not, because the per-entity transition sets have never been written down.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None applied. See the decision required.
findings.verification_method: Property-based test over every entity/state pair.
findings.acceptance_criteria: No transition is reachable for an entity type that does not define it.
findings.regression_risk: Medium — requires auditing every call site.
findings.decision_required: Now narrowed to the 28 synthetic keys only. They describe order, sample, crossmatch and reaction lifecycles, and none of those entities is ever passed to transition(); order, sample and reaction have no lifecycle enum at all. Those 28 rows govern nothing today and would begin governing — and colliding — the moment the corresponding entity is wired up. The mechanical keying must land in the same change as the attribution.

findings.title: The changed-files quality gate reported PASS when MyPy had failed to execute
findings.description: scripts/quality_changed_files_gate.py printed '0 diagnostics' and PASS while MyPy exited 2 without analysing anything. Two causes combined: run_mypy parsed diagnostics regardless of the exit code, so a failed run contributed an empty list that read as clean; and execution_error_regression only fired when the head's error DIFFERED from the baseline's, which is never the case when both sides run in the same environment. A tool that never ran was certifying the change.
findings.root_cause: Zero diagnostics was treated as evidence of cleanliness without first establishing that the tool actually ran. The gate shelled out to a bare 'mypy' on PATH, which can resolve to an interpreter lacking the project dependencies MyPy must import to load its SQLAlchemy and Pydantic plugins.
findings.evidence: Reproduced at d9fdd988: the pre-fix gate printed 'baseline.mypy_changed: 0 diagnostics ... QUALITY_CHANGED_FILES_GATE: PASS' while returncode was 2 with "No module named 'sqlalchemy'". Post-fix the same comparison reports real counts (mypy_changed 170 -> 135) and PASS.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly.
findings.security_impact: A green gate is evidence a reviewer relies on. Any type regression, including one weakening a security or tenant-isolation path, could pass unexamined.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None directly.
findings.operational_impact: False confidence in the merge gate.
findings.intersections: Generalises beyond MyPy: any executable check whose empty output is read as success without first proving it ran.
findings.recommended_fix: Distinguish 'ran and found nothing' from 'did not run'. A failed run yields no diagnostics at all and blocks; an unmeasured baseline also blocks, because non-regression cannot be established against nothing.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: ToolResult.measured; diagnostics gated on successful execution for MyPy as they already were for Ruff; execution_blockers replacing execution_error_regression; a distinct BLOCKED status; and MyPy invoked through sys.executable -m so it runs in the same environment as the dependencies it imports.
findings.verification_method: scripts/tests/test_quality_changed_files_gate.py: exit 0 with no findings passes; exit 1 with findings is counted as a regression; exits 2, 3 and -11 yield no diagnostics and block, including when baseline and head fail identically. BATCH-1 added explicit DID_NOT_RUN and UNMEASURED states to the machine-readable report, with diagnostic_count null rather than 0 for an unmeasured run. 20 tests.
findings.acceptance_criteria: No tool execution failure can produce a PASS.
findings.regression_risk: The gate now surfaces pre-existing execution failures that were previously silent. Verified not to affect CI: the local block was Python 3.11 failing to parse PEP 695 syntax in backend/app/clinical_gateway/contracts.py; CI runs 3.12 and the same run completes (confirmed under 3.13, exit 0).

findings.title: The pharmacy warehouse is modelled in the schema but implemented nowhere
findings.description: pharmacy_warehouses is referenced by four columns (pharmacy_stores.warehouse_id, pharmacy_stock_levels.warehouse_id, pharmacy_inventory_transfers.from_warehouse_id and .to_warehouse_id) and the org model names warehouse_officer and warehouse_manager roles, yet no endpoint, service, seed, demo generator or migration ever creates a Warehouse or a Store. The columns are reachable from the API but unusable: any value fails the foreign key because no row can exist. receive_transfer moves stock by store only, ignoring the transfer table's own warehouse columns. A third, parallel location representation exists as a free-text 'location' VARCHAR on batches, stock, stores and warehouses.
findings.root_cause: The physical schema was drafted for a warehouse/store hierarchy that was never implemented, and no ADR ever decided whether it should be. P0-2 Phase 2A classified warehouse_id as RECONCILE (keep) rather than REMOVE_FROM_ORM, so M4 preserved it faithfully without resolving what it means.
findings.evidence: On a migrated database at 20260912_0001: pharmacy_warehouses and pharmacy_stores both have 0 rows; inserting a stock row with warehouse_id=42 raises a foreign-key violation. Warehouse and Store are imported nowhere outside backend/app/pharmacy/models.py. pharmacy_warehouses has exactly one outbound FK (lab_id -> labs) and no FK to national_facilities, so it is lab-scoped, not facility-scoped. pharmacy_stores.warehouse_id is nullable, so store does not determine warehouse. pharmacy_stock_levels carries no CHECK constraint, so nothing prevents a stock row whose store_id and warehouse_id disagree.
findings.clinical_impact: None today: the feature is inert. If implemented incorrectly later, stock attributed to the wrong location can misdirect dispensing.
findings.security_impact: GET /inventory/stock-levels accepts warehouse_id and store_id as internal integer keys on the public API surface, which CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §3 forbids. Currently unreachable because no such row can exist.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The schema permits stock rows whose store_id and warehouse_id contradict each other. Unreachable today only because neither can be set to a valid value.
findings.operational_impact: Dead schema that reads as a supported feature. Two role names promise a subsystem that does not exist.
findings.dependencies: Depends on deciding whether pharmacy inventory locations are lab-scoped or facility-scoped, and on reconciling the free-text 'location' column.
findings.intersections: P0-2-M4-GAP-STOCK-WAREHOUSE; NR-016's stock uniqueness constraint uq_pharmacy_stock; CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §2 and §3.
findings.contradictions: The schema, the role catalogue and the transfer table all assume warehouses exist; every code path assumes they do not.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the question before writing any code. Either (a) warehouse is first-class: give it creation endpoints, a public identifier per CANONICAL_DRUG_CONTRACT §2, a decision on lab- versus facility-scoping, a rule tying stock.warehouse_id to stock.store_id, and a resolution of the free-text location column; or (b) it is not: retire the two tables and four columns deliberately through a migration. Do not implement either speculatively.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: None available — the fix requires a domain decision. What was done instead: the analysis and its evidence are recorded in docs/pharmacy-platform/P0-2-M4-GAP-STOCK-WAREHOUSE.md, and two regression guards assert that warehouse_id stays out of the stock uniqueness key and that the premise behind that conclusion (no creation path exists) still holds.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_pharmacy_inventory_identity_postgres.py::test_warehouse_is_not_part_of_stock_identity and ::test_nothing_can_create_a_warehouse_or_a_store. The second fails the moment a creation path is added, forcing the identity question to be re-answered rather than inherited.
findings.acceptance_criteria: An ADR decides whether the pharmacy warehouse exists, and the schema and code agree with it.
findings.regression_risk: None from the guards. Adding warehouse_id to uq_pharmacy_stock would be a regression, not a fix: the column is unconditionally NULL, so under NULLS NOT DISTINCT it adds a constant, and under default NULL semantics it would make every stock row trivially distinct and silently void the constraint.
findings.related_adrs: None. ADR-017 concerns the National Health Data Warehouse and is unrelated despite the name collision.

findings.title: One name, two incompatible identifier schemes: _ulid() is a ULID in 2 places and a truncated UUID4 in 13
findings.description: Fifteen functions in the tree are named _ulid(). Thirteen return str(uuid.uuid4()).replace('-', '').upper()[:26] — the first 26 hex characters of a random UUID4, with no timestamp prefix, no Crockford base32 and no monotonic ordering. Two are genuine ULIDs (48-bit millisecond timestamp plus 80 random bits, Crockford base32, time-sortable). Identifiers minted under one name are therefore not mutually ordered, and a call site does not reveal which scheme it gets. Every declarative base uses the fake one; the genuine implementation mints no primary keys.
findings.root_cause: A ULID was intended; a truncated UUID4 was written and copied. A correct implementation was later written twice, under the same name, without reconciling the copies.
findings.evidence: AST scan of every _ulid() definition under backend/: 13 truncated-UUID4 bodies (app/{care_continuum,citizen_platform,clinical,ehr,identity,national,nursing}/base.py, two national notification-platform modules, three staticmethods in app/identity/certificates/services.py, and one test helper) and 2 genuine ULIDs (app/services/consent_service.py:30, app/services/mpi/resolver.py:57), both using the standard Crockford alphabet '0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ'. An earlier draft of this finding claimed all fifteen were identical; that was wrong and is corrected here.
findings.affected_components: backend/app/*/base.py (15 modules) and every model keyed on String(26)
findings.affected_users: None directly — this is a performance and design defect, not a correctness one.

findings.data_integrity_impact: None. Keys remain unique.
findings.operational_impact: The 13 fake keys pay the full 26-byte cost of a string primary key while delivering none of ULID's only benefit — time-ordered index insertion. Random insertion order causes B-tree page splits a monotonic key would avoid. Separately, two identifier populations under one name cannot be ordered against each other.
findings.scalability_impact: Grows with row count. This is the measured basis for choosing INTEGER/BIGINT keys for the national core rather than copying the VARCHAR shape.
findings.intersections: NR-003 (pharmacy PK type divergence, same key shape).
findings.recommended_fix: Pick one implementation and give the other a different name. For new tables, follow the identity contract (INTEGER/BIGINT internal key, UUID4 public id). Do not retype live keys merely for consistency.

findings.verification_method: An AST guard pinning the 13/2 split, plus an ordering test asserting that two identifiers generated a second apart sort in creation order — which the 13 fail and the 2 pass.

findings.evidence: AST route scan plus a read of the service. findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED. No second idempotency mechanism was introduced.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/blood_bank/test_sample_transition_idempotency.py — 4 tests, 3 fail with the fix reverted

findings.evidence: Executed at head 20260912_0001: zero tables matching 'ehr%' among 423; ORM SELECT on MedicationRequest and MedicationAdministration both raise UndefinedTable; none of national_patients/citizens/encounters/practitioners exists (NR-022), and every ehr_medication_* model declares real ForeignKeys to them; no ehr_medication_* model has a lab_id column although six caller sites filter on one; all four are String(26)-keyed against INTEGER-keyed Pharmacy and Nursing. findings.title: A pharmacy point-of-sale sale naming a patient writes to a table that does not exist
findings.description: PharmacyService.create_pos_sale builds an EHR MedicationDispense for every sale line whenever the caller supplies patient_id or citizen_id, and the POS request model accepts both. The INSERT targets ehr_medication_dispenses, which does not exist, so the sale cannot commit. Sales without a patient context are unaffected, which is why the existing POS tests pass and CI is green.
findings.root_cause: The POS path was written against the EHR medication domain while Pharmacy already owns pharmacy_dispense_records. Two dispensing models, one of them unbuilt.
findings.evidence: app/pharmacy/services.py imports MedicationDispense and constructs it under `if record_patient_id:`; app/pharmacy/routes.py exposes patient_id and citizen_id on the POS sale request. to_regclass('public.ehr_medication_dispenses') is NULL at head. Pinned by test_pharmacy_point_of_sale_writes_to_a_table_that_does_not_exist.
findings.clinical_impact: A dispense cannot be recorded against a named patient at the point of sale.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No data is lost — the transaction fails before commit.
findings.security_impact: None directly; the EHR model carries no lab_id, so building it as declared would remove tenant scoping from this path.
findings.recommended_fix: Write the dispense to pharmacy_dispense_records, which is built, lab-scoped and INTEGER-keyed. No schema change. Sequence it first in MED-001.
findings.resolution: The POS path now writes a canonical Pharmacy DispenseRecord to pharmacy_dispense_records instead of an EHR MedicationDispense. The table is built, lab-scoped and INTEGER-keyed, and its patient_id is a real foreign key to patients(id) — which the sale already carries as billing_patient_id. The sale's canonical patient_id/citizen_id are unconstrained strings and remain on the sale, which owns them, so no identity semantics were lost. No schema change and no migration: pharmacy_sale_lines.medication_dispense_id was already String(26) and now carries the Pharmacy dispense id, so the API response shape is unchanged. is_verified is deliberately False — a counter sale has no independent verifier, and record_manual_dispense remains the path that requires one.
findings.verification: tests/test_pharmacy_pos.py 8 passed (sale without patient context writes no dispense; citizen_id alone still records one; canonical persistence and the sale-line link; tenant isolation across two laboratories; a failed sale leaves no dispense and no stock movement, checked through a nested savepoint; and a source guard that the EHR model is not reachable from Pharmacy). Pharmacy/billing/clinical selection 322 passed, 1 skipped. CI clinical safety gate set 35 passed.

findings.title: The user_id token claim is ambiguous across two identity tables
findings.description: get_current_user resolves the user_id claim by querying LabUser first and falling back to User. Both tables have independent INTEGER primary keys and the token carries no discriminator, so a token claiming user_id = N resolves to lab_users.id = N whenever one exists — silently, with that laboratory user's role and lab_id.
findings.root_cause: Two legacy identity tables behind a single undiscriminated claim. The platform models the discriminator everywhere else — get_perm_version takes account_kind='user'|'lab', and LegacyAccountLinkSource is exactly {user, lab_user} — but the token does not carry it.
findings.evidence: app/security/dependencies.py:65-71. Measured at head: users = 0 rows, lab_users = 6, so the ambiguity is latent rather than live. AUTH-002 flow harness: a legacy token resolves through the legacy dependency with 200 OK and no kind check. AUTH-003 found a second instance the AUTH-002 sweep missed: the mobile refresh rotation (routes/mobile.py) resolved the same way and mints from what it resolves, so a citizen refresh token could be exchanged for an access token carrying a laboratory user's role and tenant.
findings.security_impact: Account-takeover class. Unexploitable only while the users table is empty; it becomes exploitable the moment citizens are registered.
findings.clinical_impact: A citizen token could resolve to a laboratory user's role and tenant.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Cross-tenant read/write under a mistaken identity.
findings.recommended_fix: Resolve through LegacyAccountLink using source_kind during the AUTH-002 bridge. Do not add a separate discriminator claim to the legacy token as a parallel mechanism.
findings.resolution: Tokens now carry `act` — the same {user, lab} discriminator already used by perm_ver_key and LegacyAccountLinkSource — and resolve_token_subject() selects exactly one identity table. Pre-existing tokens without `act` still resolve by search but fail closed when the id exists in both tables. Applied at every mint site (login staff and citizen, /citizen/login, mobile refresh, demo) and every resolve site (get_current_user, logout, mobile refresh). Deviation from the AUTH-002 action (carry source_kind through the bridge instead) is declared in docs/architecture/auth-identity-hardening.md §1: the bridge is blocked, and `act` carries the same discriminator the bridge will read rather than a parallel one.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_auth_identity_discriminator.py — 13 tests including a colliding-identity fixture (id 770035 in both tables), fail-closed cases, legacy-compatibility cases, two structural guards against re-introduction, and revocation precision. Negative proof executed: removing the fail-closed branch and restoring the mobile fallback both fail the suite. Full suite 2960 passed, 34 skipped.

findings.title: The test schema is built from ORM metadata, so tests pass against tables no migration creates
findings.description: backend/tests/conftest.py builds the test database with _ddl_meta.create_all(engine) from the ORM metadata rather than by running migrations. Any table that exists as a model but has no migration is therefore present in tests and absent in production. The pharmacy POS tests exercised patient-linked sales and passed for exactly this reason while the same call could not commit against a migrated database.
findings.root_cause: Two sources of schema truth — ORM metadata for tests, migrations for production — with no gate asserting they agree. This is the mechanism that let NR-026, NR-032 and NR-034 all reach a green suite.
findings.evidence: conftest.py line 147: _ddl_meta.create_all(engine). test_pharmacy_pos.py asserted MedicationDispense rows keyed on citizen_id and passed, although ehr_medication_dispenses does not exist at head and no migration creates it.
findings.affected_components: backend/tests/conftest.py, and every test relying on the db fixture
findings.data_integrity_impact: None directly; the risk is undetected production defects.
findings.security_impact: A tenancy defect in a model with no migration would also go undetected.
findings.recommended_fix: Do not switch the whole suite to migrations — that is slow and would be a large change. Add a gate that asserts every table in the ORM DDL metadata either has a migration or is on a reviewed exclusion list, in the same fail-closed style as tests/test_alembic_metadata_registry.py. The exclusion list makes each unbuilt model an explicit, named decision rather than an invisible one.
findings.next_batch: TEST-002 (make the gate binding; needs CI approval)
findings.resolution: backend/tests/test_schema_fidelity.py adds the ORM to migration direction that was missing. Every ORM table must be migration-backed or named in a 198-entry ledger grouped by owning base with its disposition; a module in a migration-backed domain must not import a model from a domain the chain does not build (sixteen such importers are declared); and the gate refuses to report a pass unless the dialect is PostgreSQL, alembic_version exists, and no declared-unbuilt table is present, so a create_all() schema fails loudly instead of passing silently. create_all() is not banned — it remains correct for unit tests that make no schema claim.
findings.verification: Proven by making each defect real and reverting: adding an ORM model with no migration fails the ledger check by name; restoring the EHR import in pharmacy/services.py fails the cross-generation check with 'That is NR-034 happening again'; pointing the gate at a database without alembic_version refuses to pass. 7 tests green against migrated PostgreSQL.
findings.residue: The gate is now binding. TEST-001.1 appended tests/test_schema_fidelity.py to the 'Verify workspace schema on PostgreSQL' step of the PostgreSQL migration and schema gate job in iam-hardening.yml, which already builds a postgres:16.4 service, runs alembic upgrade head and exports MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL. CI log on ef58331c shows 'tests/test_schema_fidelity.py .......' and '11 passed', up from 4 collected items, with the job green. The step carries no continue-on-error, so a gate failure fails the job. Marginal cost about 10 seconds. Four other migration-backed suites remain unbound and are recommended for the same one-line treatment: test_alembic_metadata_registry.py, test_nursing_domain_contract.py, test_nursing_runtime.py and test_ehr_medication_dependency_p0.py. The shared db fixture is unchanged, so tests claiming API, clinical, tenant and security fidelity still run on SQLite built by create_all(); the gate stops new unbuilt tables and new cross-generation dependencies rather than converting those tests.

findings.title: Assurance was one scale across four independent verification purposes
findings.description: VerificationPolicy mapped each method to a bare level on one L0-L5 ladder and AssuranceEngine.level_for() took the maximum across all results. organization_registry sat at L4 and official_identity at L2, so an account whose organization was verified out-ranked one whose holder's identity was proven, and require(results, L2) meaning 'we know who this person is' was satisfied by an organization check.
findings.root_cause: Four independent questions - contact, identity, professional, organization - scored on one totally-ordered scale. The persisted VerificationRecordType separated them correctly all along; only the scoring collapsed them.
findings.evidence: Measured at head: level_for([organization_registry verified]) = L4 and require([...], AssuranceLevel.L2) PASSED. A second vocabulary had the same defect by averaging: AssuranceService._calculate_overall(IAL1, AAL3, FAL3) = IAL2, so authentication strength lifted identity assurance.
findings.security_impact: An organization or licence check could satisfy a demand for proven personal identity. Latent: no production module consumed either engine, so the first consumer would have inherited it.
findings.clinical_impact: Would have applied to any future gate on identity before health-data access.
findings.recommended_fix: Score per purpose; require the purpose as an argument so an omitted purpose fails closed.
findings.resolution: AssuranceProfile holds one level per VerificationPurpose; VerificationPolicy maps method to (purpose, level); level_for/require take the purpose explicitly and raise TypeError without it; L4/L5 removed. Documented as ADR-026.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_assurance_boundaries.py (15 tests) plus rewritten tests/identity/test_verification_hardening_phase3.py. Negative proof: folding organization_registry back onto the identity purpose fails 2 tests. Full suite 2977 passed, 34 skipped.

findings.title: The client supplies its own identity assurance level, assessor and evidence
findings.description: POST /niam/trust/assurance-profiles accepts ial, aal, fal, assessed_by and evidence as caller-supplied parameters and writes them with status='active'. No verification record is consulted, no check binds the caller to the person_id, and the caller names its own assessor.
findings.root_cause: The assurance profile is written from the request rather than derived from verification evidence.
findings.evidence: inspect.signature(create_assurance_profile) exposes ial/aal/fal/assessed_by/evidence; AssuranceService.assign_profile writes them unchanged. app/identity/trust/services.py references neither VerificationRecord nor AssuranceEngine.
findings.security_impact: Identity assurance can be asserted rather than earned. Latent in the same way NR-035 was: the route sits behind NIAM authentication, which the application cannot reach with a legacy token, so it goes live with the AUTH-002 bridge.
findings.clinical_impact: Any future gate on assurance before clinical access would be satisfiable by assertion.
findings.recommended_fix: Derive the profile from VerificationRecord rows via AssuranceEngine; make ial/aal/fal server-computed and never request fields; bind the caller's authority to assert for that person_id.
findings.verification: Behavioural, against migrated PostgreSQL, now that the path executes: test_an_account_with_no_identity_evidence_gets_the_floor_assurance_nr038 (no record -> IAL1/AAL1/FAL1, evidence derived_from=niam_verification_records, assessed_by is the actor); test_only_a_real_verification_record_raises_the_level_nr038 (the level moves only after VerificationWorkflow writes a verified record through the real state machine); test_the_overall_assurance_is_the_weakest_axis_not_the_average_nr038 (a raised IAL does not lift the overall while AAL and FAL are at the floor); test_asserting_for_another_account_needs_an_administrative_assignment_nr038 (the route gate refuses with 403). The static half — ial/aal/fal/assessed_by/evidence are not request parameters — remains pinned in test_identity_assurance_boundaries.py.
findings.resolution: POST /niam/trust/assurance-profiles now names a subject and nothing else. ial is derived from the account's identity-purpose assurance via AssuranceEngine; aal and fal sit at the floor because neither is derivable from verification records; assessed_by is the authenticated actor; acting for another account requires an active administrative assignment. _calculate_overall no longer averages IAL/AAL/FAL - the overall is the weakest axis, so authentication strength can no longer lift an unproofed identity. FINALIZATION CORRECTION: the route cannot execute at all (NR-044) — get_db yields a sync Session while the service awaits session.execute — so the behavioural proof AUTH-005 Phase 2 required cannot be produced for this path, and the finding is PARTIALLY VERIFIED rather than VERIFIED. It also means NR-038 was never exploitable: the route raised before a client-authored assurance level could be persisted.

findings.title: users.is_verified means both 'a code was received' and 'identity confirmed'
findings.description: POST /auth/verification/confirm sets users.is_verified from a six-digit email or SMS code - contact assurance. PUT /admin/citizens/{id}/verify sets the same column and documents itself as identity confirmation. Nothing records which occurred, so no reader can tell them apart.
findings.root_cause: One boolean serving two different verification purposes, with no method, assurance or evidence recorded.
findings.evidence: routes/verification.py sets user.is_verified = True after OTP confirmation; routes/admin.py verify_citizen sets citizen.is_verified = True with audit detail 'Citizen identity verified'. Neither writes a VerificationRecord. CitizenRelationshipService.activate - which links an account to a citizen and a patient with a scope - refuses unless 'not source.is_verified', reading the OTP-set boolean while its message means identity.
findings.security_impact: A health-data linkage gate is misinformed about what was proven. Activation is ministry-authorized, so this is a misinformed human decision rather than self-service escalation.
findings.clinical_impact: A ministry actor may link health data believing identity was established when only contact was.
findings.recommended_fix: Write VerificationRecord rows with purpose and assurance from both paths, and re-gate the linkage on identity assurance rather than the boolean.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py - 17 tests on the migrated PostgreSQL schema. Negative proof: trusting the stored assurance column and removing the threshold fails six tests.
findings.next_batch: Needs a policy decision on what assurance a ministry actor must have before linking health data.
findings.resolution: CitizenRelationshipService.activate no longer reads users.is_verified. It calls can_link_health_identity, which walks legacy id + account kind -> exactly one validated LegacyAccountLink -> canonical Account -> identity-purpose VerificationRecord -> AssuranceEngine -> assurance >= L2, and refuses with an audited reason code at every gap. The ministry authorization is unchanged and still required: it authorizes the operation, the record establishes the person. users.is_verified keeps its legacy contact semantics.

findings.title: The canonical verification domain is built, migrated and wired to nothing
findings.description: niam_verification_records is migration-backed and physically present with 0 rows. The record model, state machine, provider protocol, NotConnectedProvider and AssuranceEngine all exist and are unit-tested. No module in app/ constructs a record or calls the service, so every verification the platform actually performs happens outside the model designed to hold it.
findings.root_cause: The domain was built ahead of the flows that would use it, and the flows were built on a boolean.
findings.evidence: Repository-wide search finds VerificationRecordService referenced only by its own module.
findings.security_impact: Assurance, method, provider, expiry and revocation are unrecorded for every verification performed.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly; it is the precondition for every identity gate the cohort plan needs.
findings.recommended_fix: Wire /auth/verification and the admin identity path to write records, then derive assurance from them.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py drives request/start/apply against migrated PostgreSQL; test_identity_assurance_boundaries.py pins that the workflow uses the state machine rather than bypassing it.
findings.resolution: VerificationWorkflow creates records and advances them through the existing state machine, scoring results with VerificationPolicy rather than accepting the provider's self-report. NotConnectedProvider remains fail-closed. Correction to the AUTH-004 narrative: the domain had one reader all along - WorkspaceService._professional_eligible - and no writer, so with zero rows professional workspaces were unreachable by construction. Retro-fitting the legacy OTP path is blocked behind AUTH-F10: VerificationRecord.account_id is a non-null FK to niam_accounts, which legacy users do not have.

findings.title: MFA exists for staff only, and its service takes an undiscriminated integer id
findings.description: mfa_devices.user_id is a foreign key to lab_users.id, so TOTP, WebAuthn/passkey and recovery codes are available to staff and not to citizens. MFAService methods take a bare user_id: int with no account kind.
findings.root_cause: MFA was built for the staff identity table before the citizen table carried accounts.
findings.evidence: app/models/mfa_device.py MFADevice.user_id -> lab_users.id; MFAService signatures take user_id: int.
findings.security_impact: Citizen accounts have no second factor, so account-takeover resistance rests on a password alone. The undiscriminated id is the NR-035 shape in the MFA surface, latent because the foreign key constrains rows to lab_users.
findings.clinical_impact: A citizen account gives access to that citizen's own clinical history.
findings.recommended_fix: Carry the account kind through MFAService, and decide the citizen second-factor path (passkey preferred over SMS).

findings.evidence: app/identity/services/workspace_service.py list_eligible selected workspaces by organization_id with no join to niam_organizations.
findings.security_impact: Continued workspace access after an organization was deactivated.

findings.title: The NIAM async service layer cannot execute — there is no async engine
findings.status: RESOLVED for every reachable path (NR-044.1/.2/.3 VERIFIED); 4 modules remain inside the dead NR-050 tree
findings.description: get_db yields a synchronous sqlalchemy.orm.Session. Thirty-six modules under app/identity/ annotate AsyncSession and call `await session.execute(...)`, and no create_async_engine exists anywhere in app/. Awaiting a sync result raises TypeError before any statement reaches the database, so the trust/assurance routes, workspace eligibility, membership services and the identity repositories are unreachable at runtime.
findings.root_cause: The identity platform was written against an async session contract the application never provided. The annotations are decorative; no async engine was ever created.
findings.evidence: Measured: inspect.isasyncgenfunction(get_db) is False; SessionLocal() yields Session; `await session.execute(text('SELECT 1'))` raises TypeError: object ChunkedIteratorResult can't be used in 'await' expression. grep finds zero create_async_engine in app/ and 36 modules awaiting a session execute. No async driver (asyncpg) is installed. AST inventory at 4935bf85: 50 modules, 460 await-db call sites, 506 async defs, 131 AsyncSession annotations, 45 async context managers, 0 async for. Of 506 async defs, 251 await only the database (mechanical), 96 mix database with calls to other same-layer async functions (cascade), and exactly ONE performs genuine async I/O (identity/admin/services.py:450, httpx). Decisive runtime measurement: given the same token and the same session, get_current_niam_actor (async) raises TypeError at the DB call while get_current_niam_actor_sync executes the query and returns a correct 401. The async dependency guards the whole /niam/* router, so every NIAM route fails at the door.
findings.security_impact: Neutral-to-positive today — it is why NR-038 was never exploitable — but it means several controls that appear to exist cannot run, and any future reader may mistake unreachable code for an enforced control.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly: the health-identity linkage path is synchronous and does execute. The unreachable layer is organizational/workspace, not clinical.
findings.recommended_fix: Option B: converge on the synchronous Session. Evidence: one genuine async I/O site in 506 async functions; no measured concurrency requirement; Option A would add a second engine and pool (30 -> 60 connections against PostgreSQL's 100) and two transaction boundaries per request, creating a permanent dual architecture; and the conversion already exists in the tree as get_current_niam_actor_sync. Costs no migrations and no connections. Conversion is a separate batch in five steps, NR-044.1 first (repositories + the actor dependency), which unblocks the entire /niam/* router.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_platform_runtime.py — 9 tests, including the two-state AST ledger (now 40 modules), test_the_niam_actor_dependency_is_one_synchronous_function and test_the_repository_layer_is_synchronous. backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py — the actor dependency and the repository layer exercised against migrated PostgreSQL (test_the_niam_actor_dependency_now_authenticates_against_postgresql, test_a_locked_account_is_refused, test_a_revoked_session_is_refused, test_a_token_naming_another_session_is_refused, test_a_suspended_account_is_refused, test_the_repository_layer_reaches_postgresql). Negative proof in both directions: reverting the actor to async fails 7 tests; reverting one repository fails 3. Both reverted. NR-044.1 FINAL VERIFICATION: the architecture invariants are now enforced, not merely recorded - one synchronous engine architecture, no AsyncEngine, no second pool or sessionmaker inside app/identity/, the actor's db annotation resolved to sqlalchemy.orm.Session and bound to get_db, and the one genuine async I/O site preserved. Runtime proofs on migrated PostgreSQL 16.13 through the real FastAPI dependency graph: unauthenticated 401, malformed token 401, foreign-signed token 401, expired token 401, locked/suspended/revoked/wrong-jti/cross-account all refused, and an eight-step authorization denial ladder in which each refusal is provoked by a real row and names a different boundary. One Session is shared by the gate, the repositories and the resolver, proved by uncommitted-row visibility with the transaction still open. Four reversible perturbations failed 18, 4, 3 and 1 tests respectively; all restored. NOT PROVEN: the authorization ALLOW path, blocked by NR-045.
findings.next_batch: Nothing, unless NR-050 is decided. The four modules still in the ledger are capabilities/*/infrastructure/repository.py, whose packages raise ModuleNotFoundError; converting them means completing or retiring that tree, which is NR-050's decision.
findings.resolution: NR-044.1 converted the ten modules of app/identity/repositories/ and the actor dependency in app/identity/api/workspaces.py to the synchronous Session. No AsyncEngine, AsyncSession, asyncpg, second pool or migration was introduced. The AST ledger shrank from 50 modules to 40 — exactly the ten repositories, added: []. PRECISE REACHABILITY: get_current_niam_actor now executes against PostgreSQL, so every /niam/* route passes its gate; the route handlers are still async and still await AsyncSession-annotated services, so an individual handler still raises TypeError past the gate. /niam/* is gated, not yet served — serving it is NR-044.2 (services) and NR-044.3 (routes). NR-038 and NR-043 therefore stay PARTIALLY VERIFIED; their behavioural proof needs the service layer, not the gate. TWO BEHAVIOUR CHANGES, not refactors: (1) the converged gate keeps the sync implementation's Account.is_locked filter, which the async twin omitted, so the gate is strictly tighter than either predecessor; (2) a latent ModuleNotFoundError was fixed — IdentityRepositoryBase.count read 'from sqlalchemy.func import count', and sqlalchemy.func is an attribute of the package, not a module; it was unreachable while the layer could not execute and surfaced on the first real call. NR-044.2 converted identity/services (16 modules), identity/api (13), identity/policy_engine.py and services/clinical_scope_bridge_service.py to the synchronous Session, and deleted SyncSessionAsyncFacade — the shim that made a sync Session look awaitable so the clinical gateway could drive async services with asyncio.run() inside a request. Ledger 40 -> 20 modules, none added. No AsyncEngine, AsyncSession, asyncpg or second pool was introduced; one Engine and one sessionmaker remain, asserted by test_exactly_one_database_engine_architecture_exists. NR-044.3 converted the remaining identity sub-packages (trust, admin, compliance, federation, governance, notifications, certificates, adaptive_auth, bootstrap, workflows and their routes), reference/infrastructure (NR-049's module), and the two national repositories — task_engine and workflow_runtime — which were NOT dead: their routers are registered in factory.py and they import fine under the PYTHONPATH the application actually runs with. One Class B boundary was preserved deliberately: EnterprisePortalService.test_fhir_connection stays a coroutine because it makes a genuine httpx call to an external FHIR server; its database statements are synchronous. Ledger 20 -> 4.

findings.title: CanonicalAuditService cannot write a row, so every clinical-gateway request answers 503
findings.description: IdentityAuditEntry.uuid is NOT NULL with no default. AuditService sets id, uuid, entry_hash and previous_hash explicitly; CanonicalAuditService.record() - the writer the clinical read gateway uses for every allow and every deny - sets none of them. The INSERT violates the not-null constraint, ClinicalGatewayAuditFailure is raised, and every /api/v1/clinical/* request returns 503 regardless of whether the caller was authorized.
findings.root_cause: The v2 canonical audit writer was written against the ORM defaults it assumed rather than the columns the migration declares. It was never exercised against the migrated schema because the existing gateway tests monkeypatch the audit call.
findings.evidence: Measured on migrated PostgreSQL 16.13: asyncio.run(CanonicalAuditService(SyncSessionAsyncFacade(db)).record(...)) raises psycopg2.errors.NotNullViolation: null value in column "uuid" of relation "niam_audit_entries"; the INSERT parameters show uuid=None, entry_hash=None, previous_hash=None. GET /api/v1/clinical/patients with a valid NIAM token returns 503 UNAVAILABLE for the same reason.
findings.security_impact: Fails closed - no clinical data is returned and nothing is exposed - but the canonical audit trail for the clinical gateway is empty, and a control that cannot record is not a control. Any future reader may mistake the 503 for an infrastructure problem rather than a broken audit writer.
findings.clinical_impact: The canonical clinical read gateway is entirely non-functional. No clinician can read patients or orders through it.
findings.recommended_fix: Set id, uuid and the hash-chain fields in CanonicalAuditService.record() the way AuditService already does, or give IdentityAuditEntry a default for uuid. Then exercise the allow path against the migrated schema rather than around it.
findings.verification: Against migrated PostgreSQL 16.13: the insert that used to raise NotNullViolation now succeeds with a canonical uuid4 and a populated entry_hash; two consecutive entries chain (second.previous_hash == first.entry_hash) and CanonicalAuditService.verify() returns VALID with zero violations. Atomicity: the audit row is visible inside its own transaction and absent from another connection after rollback; record() never commits (asserted behaviourally and by source inspection). End to end over real HTTP the clinical gateway now answers 403 where it answered 503, and the denial is readable in niam_audit_entries with decision=deny, reason_code=missing_workspace, source=clinical_gateway. Negative proof: removing the column default fails 6 tests; restored. Tests in backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py.
findings.next_batch: Unblocked the clinical-gateway DENY path end to end. The ALLOW path is still blocked, but by NR-047 (Organization ORM/migration divergence), not by audit.
findings.resolution: IdentityAuditEntry.uuid now carries the canonical default (_audit_entry_uuid). The column is the single authority for every writer of niam_audit_entries rather than a second generator beside AuditService's; AuditService still passes its own value, which takes precedence, so v1 behaviour is byte-identical. `uuid` is deliberately absent from CanonicalAuditService._canonical_payload, so populating it cannot alter any entry hash, past or future. No migration: a Python-side column default emits no DDL (compiled CREATE TABLE for the column is unchanged, 'uuid VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL'). No constraint weakened, no field made nullable, no second hash-chain implementation, no separate commit.

findings.title: The NIAM actor dependency does not consult UserSession.expires_at
findings.description: get_current_niam_actor filters on UserSession.is_active but never on UserSession.expires_at, which is NOT NULL and is set at login. A session row whose expires_at is in the past still authenticates, provided the bearer token itself has not expired.
findings.root_cause: The predicate was written from the account's standing and the session's active flag; the row's own declared lifetime was not part of the conjunction.
findings.evidence: Measured on migrated PostgreSQL: with session_row.expires_at set one day in the past and is_active still True, get_current_niam_actor returns the actor rather than raising 401. NOT a NR-044.1 regression - the converted query is byte-for-byte the pre-existing get_current_niam_actor_sync, and the async twin omitted the check too (it also omitted Account.is_locked, which the conversion kept).
findings.security_impact: Bounded by the access token's own exp, which IS enforced (JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES, default 15). The gap matters only where a session is intended to expire sooner than the tokens minted against it - for example an administrative session cut short, or a shorter server-side session policy.
findings.clinical_impact: Indirect: the clinical gateway depends on this actor, so a session past its declared expiry could still reach authorization.
findings.recommended_fix: Add `or_(UserSession.expires_at.is_(None), UserSession.expires_at > now)` to the actor's filter, matching how Membership.expires_at is already handled in ClinicalGatewayContextResolver.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py::test_the_gate_does_not_consult_the_session_row_expiry asserts today's behaviour so that adding the check fails there and the test is rewritten to pin the fix.

findings.title: The Organization ORM does not match the organizations table, so the clinical allow path cannot resolve operational scope
findings.description: app/models/organization.py::Organization declares org_id, org_type, parent_org_id and updated_at, none of which exist on the migrated `organizations` table (which has organization_id and organization_type). Any ORM query selecting the Organization entity raises UndefinedColumn. The four phantom columns are exactly NIAMOrganization's vocabulary: the operational model was written in the NIAM model's names. Two live consequences: the clinical authorization allow path cannot resolve operational scope, and the national bootstrap has never run.
findings.root_cause: The operational Organization ORM adopted the neighbouring NIAM organization model's field names without its semantics. `organizations` was created 2026-07-22 by 20260722_0001_authorization_expansion with organization_id/organization_type; niam_organizations was created 2026-07-23 by 20260723_0001_niam_identity_platform_tables with org_id/org_type/parent_org_id/updated_at. No rename or removal ever occurred - across all 106 migrations nothing references organizations.org_id, .org_type, .parent_org_id or .updated_at.
findings.evidence: PHYSICAL: organizations has integer serial id, organization_id varchar(100) UNIQUE, organization_type, tenant_id -> tenants.id, and FOUR inbound foreign keys - facilities, users, role_assignments and niam_assignments.clinical_organization_resource_id. NIAM's own assignment table references it, so it is the referenced authority for clinical organization identity, not a projection. OWNERSHIP: exactly one ORM class maps to organizations; no duplicate authority. national_organizations has no physical table. RUNTIME: 14 modules import Organization. The authorization path uses only id, is_active and tenant_id - all present - and fails only because select(Facility, Organization, Tenant) selects whole entities. The phantom columns are used ONLY by app/core/bootstrap/ (org_id 6 sites, org_type 2, parent_org_id 1). BOOTSTRAP: run_bootstrap is called from startup_guard _run_national_bootstrap inside try/except Exception logged 'non-fatal'; executed against the migrated schema it fails on SELECT ... organizations.org_id ... WHERE organizations.org_id = 'org-iraq-moh', so the platform boots with system_ready True and never seeds the ministry, directorates, organizations, facilities or laboratories. organizations having 0 rows is the symptom, not evidence of disuse.
findings.security_impact: Fails closed on both paths. The misclassification is the concern: clinical_gateway/context.py:164 converts ANY exception into ClinicalGatewayBlocked('invalid_context'), rendered as 403, so an UndefinedColumn is indistinguishable from a genuine policy denial. authorization_decision.py:200 by contrast maps failures to deny(internal_failure), which is correctly labelled.
findings.clinical_impact: No clinician can complete an authorized clinical read through the canonical gateway, and a fresh deployment has no seeded ministry, directorate, organization, facility or laboratory records.
findings.recommended_fix: Option A + B as one small batch. A: map the ORM attributes onto the real column names (Column('organization_id', ...) keeps the Python attribute stable so bootstrap needs no edit) - no migration. B: one additive, nullable, idempotent migration for parent_org_id varchar(100) and updated_at timestamptz, the two columns that genuinely do not exist. No rename, no drop, no type change, no data movement; organizations is empty. Rejected: C (select columns instead of entities - hides the drift per call site and leaves bootstrap broken); D (merge with niam_organizations - the FK graph shows two distinct entities with a deliberate bridge); E (defer into NR-022 - separable, and would delay a live bootstrap defect).
findings.verification: Against migrated PostgreSQL 16.13. SCHEMA: declared-minus-physical and physical-minus-declared are both empty. QUERIES: select(Organization); Organization+Tenant; Facility+Organization+Tenant; the exact ClinicalAuthorizationContextService query; the bootstrap lookup; the bootstrap org_type and parent_org_id reads - all six execute. MIGRATION: upgrade/downgrade/re-upgrade round trip, one head 20260913_0001, all four inbound foreign keys and the UNIQUE constraint preserved. BOOTSTRAP: run_bootstrap completes (ministry=1, directorates=19, permissions=92, roles=19); the ministry is at the root with parent_org_id NULL; every directorate's parent resolves to a real organization_id; no facility lacks an organization; a second pass adds zero organizations and zero facilities with no duplicate org_id. ALLOW: GET /api/v1/clinical/patients returns HTTP 200 with the workspace context echoed back, and the resolver reports the full operational scope (lab, facility, tenant). DENY: eight boundaries broken one at a time from that same otherwise-allowing context, each yielding its own reason and recovering when restored. AUDIT: exactly one clinical_gateway entry per read with uuid, entry_hash, decision=allow, and verify() VALID. NEGATIVE PROOF: reverting the ORM mapping fails 8 tests, reinstating updated_at fails 8, rolling back the migration fails 7; all restored.
findings.discovered_by: NR-045 repair (attempting the NR-044.1 allow-path proof)
findings.next_batch: Unblocked the NR-044.1 authorization ALLOW proof. Separate observation, not folded in: lims_departments gains 16 rows on a second bootstrap pass and is stable from the third - a pre-existing seeder behaviour in a different seeder, recorded rather than scope-crept.
findings.resolution: Three of the four phantom columns were naming, one was real, and they were treated differently. org_id and org_type are now MAPPED onto the existing physical columns (Column('organization_id', ...) / Column('organization_type', ...)), so every caller in app/core/bootstrap/ is unchanged and no physical column was renamed. updated_at was REMOVED from the ORM rather than added to the table, because nothing reads, writes or serialises it - adding a column only to make a model and a table look alike would be drift in the other direction. parent_org_id was ADDED by migration 20260913_0001 because the bootstrap genuinely seeds a ministry-to-directorate hierarchy through it: VARCHAR(100) nullable indexed, matching OrganizationDef.parent_org_id: str|None which carries a public identifier - deliberately NOT NIAMOrganization's integer self-FK of the same name. No foreign key was declared, recorded as a deliberate omission. The migration is additive, nullable, idempotent and reversible; no rename, no drop, no type change, no data movement.

findings.title: The clinical gateway reported any internal fault as an authorization denial
findings.description: ClinicalGatewayContextResolver.resolve wrapped the context-service call in `except Exception` and converted every exception into ClinicalGatewayBlocked('invalid_context'), rendered as HTTP 403. A schema fault, a dropped connection and a programming error were therefore indistinguishable from a genuine policy denial — in the response, in the logs and in the canonical audit row, which recorded reason_code=invalid_context either way.
findings.root_cause: A broad catch written to keep the gateway fail-closed. It does fail closed; what it also does is destroy the distinction between 'the policy refused you' and 'this service is broken', which is the distinction an operator needs first.
findings.evidence: NR-047 is the worked example: `column organizations.org_id does not exist` reached the client as a 403 that looked exactly like an authorization denial, and stayed hidden behind that appearance until the allow path was built. NR-044's `TypeError: object ChunkedIteratorResult can't be used in 'await' expression` was swallowed by the same handler.
findings.security_impact: No weakening — every affected request was refused. The cost is diagnostic and audit-integrity: an availability fault was recorded in the immutable audit chain as an access decision that was never made.
findings.clinical_impact: A clinician reading 'access denied' when the true cause was a broken database mapping has no route to the real problem, and neither does whoever reviews the audit trail.
findings.recommended_fix: Catch only the context service's own denial vocabulary.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py::test_a_database_fault_is_no_longer_reported_as_a_policy_denial raises a real sqlalchemy OperationalError from inside the context service and asserts it propagates; ::test_a_genuine_context_denial_is_still_translated_to_invalid_context asserts the other half; the denial ladder continues to produce invalid_context for real context failures. tests/test_identity_platform_runtime.py::test_the_gateway_does_not_report_a_database_fault_as_a_policy_denial pins the handler itself.
findings.resolution: The handler now catches (ClinicalAuthorizationContextError, ClinicalScopeBridgeError) — the two ValueError hierarchies the context service and the scope bridge raise to mean 'refused'. Anything else propagates and surfaces as a 500: still denied, but as a fault rather than as a decision, and no longer written into the audit chain as one.

findings.title: The NR-044 ledger could not see a module that stored its session as self._session
findings.status: OPEN (module unconverted; the guard blind spot is FIXED)
findings.description: The AST guard that enumerates unreachable async database modules matched a session owner only when it was a bare name in _SESSION_OWNERS or an attribute chain ending in `.session` or `.db`. app/reference/infrastructure/repositories.py keeps its session on `self._session` and awaits it 20+ times, so it was invisible to the ledger for as long as the ledger has existed.
findings.root_cause: The owner rule was written from the modules that were already known, so it encoded their naming conventions rather than the property being measured.
findings.evidence: Widening the rule to also accept `._session` and `.facade` raised the module count from 19 to 20; the one addition is reference/infrastructure/repositories.py, which declares `def __init__(self, session: AsyncSession) -> None: self._session = session` and then `await self._session.execute(...)` throughout. app/identity/services/device_service.py had the same shape and was only in the ledger because of unrelated lines.
findings.security_impact: None directly. The cost is that a guard designed to make unreachable code visible was under-reporting, which is how NR-044 stayed hidden in the first place.
findings.clinical_impact: None established — reference/ is reference-data infrastructure, not a clinical path.
findings.recommended_fix: Two parts, one done here: widen the guard (done), and convert reference/infrastructure/repositories.py with the rest of NR-044.3 (not done).
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_platform_runtime.py — _SESSION_OWNERS and the suffix test now cover both forms, and reference/infrastructure/repositories.py is named in DECLARED_UNREACHABLE_ASYNC_DB_MODULES with the reason.

findings.title: Nine of the ten packages under app/capabilities/ cannot import, and nine have live frontend routes
findings.description: app/capabilities/ holds ten packages, 267 Python modules, 4,832 lines. NINE cannot be imported; the tenth (fhir_interoperability) is complete and live. The nine are not orphans: frontend-v3 ships nine routes and nine pages for them, behind RoleGuards gated on dashboard:read, each calling a backend endpoint that factory.py never registers.
findings.root_cause: One generator, app/engineering/generators/capability.py, emits three independent defects: (D1) a bare top-level import in __init__.py, which makes the package unimportable — one character per file; (D2) `from backend.app...` imports that resolve only because the repository root is on sys.path; (D3) a dataclass template that places a defaulted `id` before non-default fields, raising TypeError in the four packages that declare any. The generator is still live and still emits all three.
findings.evidence: CORRECTION to the PROGRAM-EXT-001 record, which said all ten fail to import, 40 of 40 modules. That was measured with a sys.path lacking the repository root — which the application, CI and pytest all have — and sampled four module kinds. Measured in the real environment over all 267 modules: fhir_interoperability 27/27 import; the other nine 0/N. Simulating D1 alone (app/capabilities on sys.path, repository untouched) makes SIX packages import completely; the remaining four fail only on D3. HISTORY: two commits touch the tree, both 15 Aug 2026. d33021e3 added 304 files in bulk; 3b7c9b70 (PR #209) completed fhir_interoperability, and its first change was exactly `-from fhir_interoperability.capability` / `+from .capability`. REGISTRY: all ten load at boot as CapabilityDescriptors and all ten fail the PROGRAM-EXT-001 contract on the same four fields. TESTS: 20 test modules inside the tree, none collected — pytest.ini sets testpaths = tests.
findings.security_impact: None. Every non-FHIR route in the tree is unregistered, and the handlers return a hardcoded empty page.
findings.clinical_impact: Nine navigable pages — clinical foundation, encounters, providers, consent, documents — reachable by any user with dashboard:read and backed by nothing. No data risk; a credibility and usability defect in clinical navigation.
findings.recommended_fix: SPLIT, and do the cheap safety work first. Runtime: keep fhir_interoperability, treat storage_service as a real gap. Discovery: preserve the four hexagonal packages (document_management, encounter_management, provider_management, workflow_engine) — the only domain/application/infrastructure template in the repository. Blocked: the rest, on NR-051 canonical owners and on where clinical entities live. Independently of all that, fix the generator (NR-053) and decide what the nine orphan frontend routes do (NR-054).
findings.verification: docs/architecture/nr-050-capability-tree-discovery.md — full inventory, runtime classification with two independent proofs per package, contract compliance, canonical-owner analysis, discovery-value scoring, git history and decision matrix.
findings.next_batch: NR-053 (fix the generator) and NR-054 (the nine orphan frontend routes) are actionable now and need no NR-050 decision. The disposition of the ten needs NR-051 and a clinical-domain-location decision.

findings.title: Six reusable concepts have between two and four implementations and no canonical owner
findings.description: Notification has four implementations, document three live plus one dead, workflow three live plus one dead, consent three live plus one dead, audit three writers, terminology two classes of the same name in different modules. The Platform Constitution's Reuse Before Build article cannot be followed because nothing states which one to reuse.
findings.root_cause: Capabilities were built per-domain as each domain needed them, with no catalogue to check first and no guard on the name.
findings.evidence: Enumerated by class name across app/. Notification: identity/notifications/services.py, platform/notifications.py, national/notification_platform/application/service.py, notifications/service.py. Document: platform/documents.py, national/document_platform/application/service.py, document_intelligence/ (4 ABCs), capabilities/document_management (dead). Workflow: platform/workflow.py, national/workflow_runtime/application/service.py, identity/workflows/engine.py, capabilities/workflow_engine (dead). Consent: identity/services/consent_service_v2.py, trust/services.py, national/security/consent_enforcement.py, capabilities/healthcare_consent (dead). Audit: identity/services/audit_service.py (v1), identity/services/canonical_audit.py (v2), platform/audit.py. Terminology: services/clinical_service.py and integration/standards/terminology.py both define TerminologyService. At the descriptor level the same duplication appears as consent_management (2.1.0) and healthcare_consent (1.0.0) both registered.
findings.security_impact: Audit is the sharp edge: CanonicalAuditService maintains the hash chain, and a third writer (platform/audit.py) that does not is a gap in an immutable trail that is supposed to have none.
findings.clinical_impact: Four notification services means four places a national clinical alert can silently fail to send, and no single place to look when one does.

findings.category: Authorization gate that could not evaluate
findings.title: The assurance-profile administrator gate filtered on a column that does not exist
findings.description: _require_assurance_administrator in app/identity/trust/routes.py is the gate that decides whether an actor may recompute an assurance profile for a different account. It filtered on Assignment.account_id, which is not a column on that model: an assignment belongs to a person, and an account reaches one through Account.identity_id -> IdentityRecord.person_id. The gate therefore raised AttributeError instead of deciding anything.
findings.root_cause: Written against the wrong side of the account/person split, and never executed. NR-044 meant the whole trust router could not run, so the error could not surface; AUTH-005 reviewed the predicate as source rather than as behaviour.
findings.evidence: `AttributeError: type object 'Assignment' has no attribute 'account_id'`, raised the first time the gate was called with a real session — which was the first time it had ever been called, in the NR-044.3 Part H proof. app/identity/models/assignment.py declares person_id, employment_id and organization_id; there is no account_id.
findings.security_impact: Fails closed, so nothing was ever wrongly allowed: the AttributeError propagates and the request is refused as a 500. The finding is that the control had never once been evaluated, so 'an active administrative assignment is required' was an untested claim, and the refusal was an availability failure wearing an authorization decision's clothes — the same confusion as NR-048.
findings.clinical_impact: None direct. Assurance profiles feed identity-linkage decisions, so a gate that cannot evaluate is a control gap in the chain that governs who may assert another person's identity assurance.
findings.recommended_fix: Join through the account's identity to the person, matching the chain ClinicalAuthorizationContextService already uses.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_identity_link_and_assurance.py::test_asserting_for_another_account_needs_an_administrative_assignment_nr038 calls the gate with a real account and session against migrated PostgreSQL and asserts HTTP 403. Negative proof: restoring `Assignment.account_id` fails that test.
findings.discovered_by: NR-044.3 Part H (proving NR-038 once the path became reachable)
findings.resolution: The gate joins Assignment to IdentityRecord on person_id and matches the actor's identity_id, keeping the identity's own active standing in the conjunction rather than trusting the account alone. The predicate is at least as strict as the one that was intended, and it now evaluates.

findings.title: The capability generator still emits all three defects that made nine packages unimportable
findings.description: app/engineering/generators/capability.py is the tool that produced app/capabilities/. It still emits: a bare top-level import at line 485 (`from {cap}.capability import ...`), which makes every generated package unimportable; `from backend.app...` at lines 8, 191 and 514, which resolves only because the repository root is on sys.path; and an entity template that places a defaulted `id` before the caller's non-default fields, raising TypeError at class creation.
findings.root_cause: The generator was written and used once, in bulk, and its output was never imported. Nothing tests the generated code, so three template bugs shipped 267 modules deep.
findings.evidence: Line 485 `from {cap}.capability import {cap_cap}Capability`; lines 8/191/514 `from backend.app...`; the entity template emits `id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid4()))` immediately before `{fields}`. All three reproduce exactly in the generated tree: nine ModuleNotFoundError, ten backend.app imports, four TypeError. PR #209 fixed the first of them by hand for one package.
findings.security_impact: None directly. The risk is that a future capability is generated broken and the breakage is only noticed when something tries to import it — which, on this evidence, may be never.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly; a clinical capability generated from this template would not run.
findings.recommended_fix: Three template edits: relative import, `app.` instead of `backend.app.`, and non-default fields before defaulted ones. Then generate one capability into a temporary directory in a test and assert it imports.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_generator.py — eight tests that RUN the generator into a temporary directory and import what comes out, rather than grepping its source. D1: the generated package imports through its own name. D2: no generated file names the backend.app root, and the package imports in a subprocess given only the application root (backend/) and not the repository root — the environment D2 broke. D3: an entity with two required and one optional field is imported and instantiated; the required fields are still required and `id` still defaults. Four negative proofs, one per defect, each failing the intended test and each restored.
findings.resolution: Six edits in app/engineering/generators/capability.py. D1: the __init__ template emits `from .capability import` instead of a bare top-level import. D2: `module_path` is `app.capabilities.<cap>` — one string that feeds the infrastructure repository's two imports, the unit test's import and the descriptor metadata — plus the two literal template imports (routes, capability) and the generator's own import of its base class. D3: the entity template puts required fields ahead of the defaulted `id`, and the field list is split by whether a field carries a default; no field is renamed, retyped, added or dropped. A fourth defect (NR-055) was found by generating rather than reading. The ten existing packages were NOT touched — their disposition remains NR-050's decision.

findings.title: Nine frontend routes call capability endpoints that are never registered
findings.description: frontend-v3 ships nine lazy-loaded routes under /capabilities/* with nine pages and nine navigation entries gated on dashboard:read. Each page issues api.get("/<capability>") — /clinical-foundation, /document-management, /encounter-management, /healthcare-consent, /provider-management, /reporting-service, /search-service, /storage-service, /workflow-engine. None of those routers is included in factory.py, and the packages that define them cannot import.
findings.root_cause: Frontend and backend scaffolding were generated from the same capability list, and only the frontend half was wired up.
findings.evidence: frontend-v3/src/routes/index.tsx lines 57-65 and 188-196; frontend-v3/src/pages/capabilities/ (nine directories); frontend-v3/src/permissions/index.ts lines 161-169; scripts/zero_drift_engine.py lines 47-56. Backend: grep for each path in factory.py returns nothing. A secondary mismatch: the stub handlers return {items, total, skip, limit} while the pages treat the response body as an array.
findings.security_impact: None — the endpoints do not exist, so nothing is exposed. Gating is dashboard:read, the broadest permission there is.
findings.clinical_impact: Nine clinical-section navigation entries lead to pages that cannot load data. No patient-safety consequence; a visible quality defect in the clinical navigation.
findings.recommended_fix: Follows the NR-050 decision. If the capabilities are completed, register the routers and fix the response-shape mismatch. If they are retired, remove the nine routes, pages, navigation entries and drift-engine entries together. Leaving navigable pages pointing at nothing is the one option that should be ruled out.
findings.verification: Not yet fixed. Measured in docs/architecture/nr-050-capability-tree-discovery.md §1.
findings.next_batch: Blocked on the NR-050 disposition, but the defect is live today either way.

findings.title: The routes template built Python function names from the hyphenated URL prefix
findings.description: _ROUTES_TPL used a single {prefix} placeholder for both the FastAPI path prefix and the five generated function names. The prefix is the capability name with underscores replaced by hyphens, so the template emitted `async def list_clinical-foundation(` — a SyntaxError. Every generated routes.py with a multi-word capability name was invalid Python.
findings.root_cause: One placeholder serving two purposes with incompatible character sets: a URL segment may contain hyphens and a Python identifier may not.
findings.evidence: Found by running the generator, not by reading it: the first Phase 3 generation produced `SyntaxError: expected '('` at routes.py line 13 for both test specs. It had been invisible because the on-disk routes.py in app/capabilities/ say `async def list_clinical_foundation` with underscores — those files were hand-corrected after generation and the template never was, so the shipped tree is not a faithful sample of what the generator produces today.
findings.security_impact: None. A module that does not parse cannot run.
findings.clinical_impact: None directly; a clinical capability generated from this template would not import.
findings.recommended_fix: Separate the two placeholders: {prefix} for the URL, {func} for the identifier.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_generator.py::test_a_minimal_capability_generates_compiles_and_imports and ::test_a_capability_with_entities_generates_every_layer compile every generated module with py_compile. Negative proof: restoring {prefix} in the function names fails both.
findings.resolution: The routes template takes {func} for the five function names, fed by the underscored capability name, while {prefix} continues to carry the hyphenated URL. Route paths and the generated API are unchanged.

findings.title: Ten sibling generators and the engineering CLI still resolve only from the repository root
findings.description: NR-053 removed the `backend.app.` root from the capability generator and from everything it emits. The same one-line self-import survives verbatim in the ten sibling generators (cqrs, crud, dto, microservice, module, plugin, project, openapi, repository, rest) and in app/engineering/productivity/cli.py, which imports all eleven through that root. Each is the identical line: `from backend.app.engineering.generators.base import BaseGenerator, GenerateResult`.
findings.root_cause: `backend.app.` resolves only where the repository root happens to be on sys.path — true under pytest and in CI (both set PYTHONPATH to workspace and workspace/backend), false for an interpreter rooted at backend/, which is how the application itself runs. The generators were written against the test environment rather than the runtime one.
findings.evidence: `grep -h 'backend\.app'` across the ten sibling generators returns exactly ten identical lines and nothing else — their templates are clean, so the defect is in how the tool loads, not in what it emits. `cd backend && python3 -c 'import app.engineering.productivity.cli'` raises ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'backend'; the same import succeeds with the repository root added. Pre-existing: last touched in d33021e3, untouched by NR-053's commit 612ab2a3.
findings.security_impact: None. No authorization, tenancy or audit path runs through these modules.
findings.clinical_impact: None. Development tooling only; no clinical request touches it.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace the eleven `backend.app.` imports with `app.` — mechanically identical to the fix NR-053 applied at capability.py line 8. Deliberately not done under NR-053, whose scope was the capability generator and its output; eleven further modules is a separate, reviewable change.
findings.verification: A subprocess rooted at backend/ with PYTHONPATH=backend imports each of the eleven modules — the same shape as test_the_generator_itself_imports_without_the_repository_root in backend/tests/test_capability_generator.py, which already proves it for capability.py.
findings.discovered_by: NR-053 (while verifying the repaired generator's own import root)
